newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: New drug may prolong cancer victims' lives - study.
newsitem.headline: New drug may prolong cancer victims' lives - study.

text.p: A new drug could significantly prolong the life of patients with advanced ovarian and small cell lung cancer (SCLC), studies presented at a cancer conference on Monday showed.
The reports were presented by U.S. drug company SmithKline Beecham at a four-day congress held by the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) in Vienna.

In a study, involving 226 patients suffering from recurrent ovarian cancer, participants were given either new drug Hycamtin or paclitaxel -- currently the most widely used agent in the treatment of the disease. The response rate of those receiving Hycamtin was 21 percent, compared with 14 percent for those who took paclitaxel.

Patient response was defined as a 50 percent or more reduction in the size of the tumour. Since the studies dealt with advanced cancer victims, survival was generally a question of months. Average survival with Hycamtin was 65 weeks, versus 59 weeks with paclitaxel.
"Hycamtin is an exciting new option that offers patients a hope for prolonged survival," said Wim ten Bokkel Huinink, consultant medical oncologist at Netherlands Cancer Institute.
"Data from this study represent a vital step forward in the management of ovarian cancer, a disease for which there is a compelling need for new therapies to treat patients," he added.
Ovarian cancer, with a rate of 25,000 new cases a year in Europe, is one of the leading causes of cancer death in women because it is often detected at a late stage.

Another study investigating the effect of Hycamtin as a single-agent treatment for advanced SCLC showed response rates of nearly 40 percent, compared to the current 20 to 30 percent rate. SCLC is particularly lethal due to its tendency to grow rapidly and spread to distant parts of the body.

The study took 101 patients with recurrent cancer, 51 of whom did not respond to initial or first-line chemotherapy, and 50 who relapsed over three months after responding to initial treatment. In the latter group response rates were 39 percent.
Overall, the duration of the response was 7.6 months, double the three months achieved by current treatment.
"This result is quite unique for this type of disease," said Andrea Ardizzoni, of the National Institute for Cancer Research, Genoa, Italy, who led the trial.

Hycamtin produced side-effects that were manageable and predictable, the main one being hematologic toxicity or a decrease in white blood cells, the company said. The drug also appeared to shrink tumours that had spread to the brain, a common occurrence in the case of SCLC.

SmithKline Beecham already has approval to market Hycamtin in the United States and Switzerland for second-line treatment of ovarian and SCLC and said approval in the European Union was in the pipeline. Phase III studies were also under way for combining Hycamtin in first-line cancer treatments.

"Because the long-term survival rates are so low and the great majority of patients experience tumour recurrence, the improvement of second-line treatment options that eventually lead to first-line advances is a critical goal for cancer researchers today," said Ardizzoni.
